why: A participant whose answers vanished mid-export is an absence, not the end of the file. `break` turns a skip into silent truncation - the researcher gets a CSV that parses, holding part of their data, with nothing saying so. This mutation survived 825 jest, 590 vitest and 16 database tests.
test: writes no row for a participant whose answers vanished mid-export

why: Ignoring `res.write`'s return value turns a slow client into an unbounded heap at the socket - reintroducing, one layer up, exactly the problem streaming removes at the database. It also disarms the listener-leak test as a side effect, because a writer that never waits never attaches a listener.
test: writes nothing more until the socket drains

why: Once the header is written the status is 200 and cannot be taken back, so a failure part-way through must destroy the connection. `end()` hands over a short CSV that parses - a researcher computing a mean over part of their data.
test: destroys the socket rather than ending it, when a row throws

why: A large export under backpressure accumulates one dead error listener per slow write - thousands of them, with the MaxListenersExceededWarning arriving long after the cause. The bug this fixed had no test, so it could come straight back.
test: leaves no listener behind, however many writes wait for a drain

why: `close` settling a pending write must RESOLVE. Rejecting routes every ordinary cancellation - a closed tab, a navigation away - into the failure path and logs it as an export failure. The bytes are identical either way, so only the log can see it.
test: treats an ordinary hangup as a hangup, not as a failure

why: Without the +1 the `>` comparison is unsatisfiable, so the 413 becomes unreachable and a 200,001-participant study quietly exports the first 200,000 as a CSV that parses. Refusal turned into truncation. Survived 824 jest and 602 vitest tests.
test: asks the database for one participant more than it will return

why: Only the refusing side was pinned, so `>` becoming `>=` survived every test in the repository - and in production that turns the largest legitimate export into a 413 naming a limit it has not reached. A boundary needs both of its sides.
test: admits a set that exactly fills the bound

why: The same +1 detector on the unbatched reader, which decides the 413 for the aggregate routes. Without it the largest studies are silently truncated into a mean, an NPS and a chart.
test: asks the database for one row more than it will return

why: The accepting side of the row bound, for the same reason as the participant one: a limit that refuses the largest legitimate read is as wrong as one that truncates it.
test: returns a result set that exactly fills the bound

why: The output is identical whether a batch fetched its hundred participants or all of them, so deleting the predicate AND its bind parameter together changes nothing anybody can see - while loading the study's whole answer set once per batch, which is the exact heap streaming exists to remove. It survived every test in four files, including the real-Postgres one, because they all compare output. ANCHOR UPDATED when !214 moved this query into `readBatch` and reindented its parameter list - the canary reported ANCHOR_MISSING rather than quietly dropping the entry, which is the whole point of requiring an exact single match.
anchor:
WHERE ${filter} AND r.session_id = ANY($${params.length + 1}::text[])
        ORDER BY r.saved_at ASC, r.id ASC
      `,
            [...params, batch]

test: asks each batch for ITS OWN hundred ids, and never for everything

why: Collapsing the per-opportunity scope to a study-wide one hands one researcher every participant another recruited, under different consent wording. It passed 588 tests in CI's configuration, because the only place the predicate is evaluated is a test that needs a real database.
test: scopes a per-opportunity export to that opportunity alone

why: Every other test in that file derives its expectations from the constant, so they all keep passing at any ceiling - including one high enough to be no ceiling at all. This number is a memory budget on a single-replica 2Gi pod, and an OOM kill here drops every live participant session.
test: holds the ceiling at the number that was decided

why: The permit is released only on the response's close. Losing that release leaks a permit for the life of the process, and two of them shut all four results routes - 503 forever, for every admin including the superadmin, reachable by a tab close.
test: gives the permit back when the response closes, however it ended

why: Loading first means a non-superadmin gets 404 for a study id that does not exist and 403 for one that does - an existence oracle over study ids, to a caller entitled to neither answer. It also makes an unentitled caller pay for a pool checkout.
test: does not read the study at all before refusing

why: `canWriteStudy` fails OPEN for an unowned study, because a write can adopt the row and a read can adopt nothing. The same shape here hands every admin the answers of any opportunity whose owner has been removed, and it passed all 293 tests in its own file.
test: refuses an opportunity nobody owns, rather than letting it fail open

why: The per-write drain bound decides how long one admin who reads nothing can refuse every other admin. Derived from the constant rather than written down, a test cannot see the constant change.
test: pins both bounds as literals

why: The whole-export wall clock is the ceiling on how long a single request can hold the only results-read permit. Before it existed there was no bound in time at all.
test: pins both bounds as literals

why: Retries spend the export's deadline. Widened or unbounded, a busy pool turns a bounded export into one that never gives the permit back - the defect the deadline exists to close, reintroduced through the fix for a different one.
test: gives up after exactly three retries rather than forever

why: `addEventListener('abort')` on a signal that has ALREADY aborted never fires, and the deadline firing during the refused query is exactly how this is reached - so without the check the backoff slept through the deadline in the common case. Same shape as `close` firing once on a response destroyed before the first write.
test: abandons its backoff the moment the export deadline fires

why: Node's `server.timeout` defaults to 0 - no bound at all on a socket that goes quiet mid-request. It is the backstop for every response that has no deadline of its own, and the assertion that catches its absence was itself reading a Node default until sentinels were added.
test: applies all three to the server it is given

why: `writeSurveyCsv` aborts its controller on every exit, and that is what lets a route test hold the signal its stand-in was handed and assert it ends up aborted. Without it the route can be given a substitute signal with the whole suite green, and the database half of the deadline silently stops being bounded.
test: aborts the signal it handed out once the export has ended
